quotes.text: A Dataverse security model only scales when it's designed around ownership and hierarchy, not around individual access requests.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: States the episode's central thesis about structural security design.

quotes.text: So treat organization depth the way you treat a master key. A small number of people need it admins, integration accounts, maybe a data steward or two.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Practical rule for restricting the most dangerous access level.

quotes.text: So there's a pattern here, and it's worth stating plainly teams own the data, users hold the work. The team is the permanent home of the record.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Memorable design principle for team-based record ownership.

quotes.text: If sharing is your main access path, the model is wrong, not the sharing the model underneath it. People are sharing because the structure doesn't put the right rows in front of the right people.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Diagnoses heavy sharing as a symptom of a flawed structure.

quotes.text: Co-Pilot and agents don't bring their own security. They read through the same model as the user who asked the question. If a user can reach a row, so can the assistant working for them.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Connects Dataverse security design to the risk surface of Copilot and agents.

takeaways: Dataverse security decides which rows a user can reach by combining identity, privilege, scope and record ownership, and access is always additive.
Business units should model real data boundaries such as legal, regulatory or contractual walls, not the org chart, and teams should own long-lived data.
Sharing, organization depth and one-off roles are shortcuts that erode the model, so roles, teams and profiles belong in solutions with reviews and auditing.
hook: Most Dataverse security problems start when access is granted one ticket at a time instead of by structure. This episode walks architects through business units, security roles, teams, ownership, column and hierarchy security, and sharing, and shows how to design a model that survives reorgs, audits and Copilot.
